newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin lets Moscow plot its own housing reforms.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin lets Moscow plot its own housing reforms.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin has approved Moscow's plans to opt out of a controversial government programme which aims to slash housing subsidies but would make life costlier for millions of Russians.

A spokesman for Moscow city hall said on Wednesday said that Yeltsin's backing for populist Mayor Yuri Luzhkov would enable the city to go ahead with its own six-point plan, deferring most municipal rent rises until 2000.

A government aide said he was not worried, but analysts said Moscow's opt-out was bound to dilute the impact of the nationwide reform, aimed at reducing massive housing subsidies put at 119 trillion roubles ($21 billion).
"Anything that defers the imposition of market discipline on a particular market, in this case housing, is a problem in the long run," said Bruce Bean, a lawyer at Coudert Brothers in Moscow.
"But if you were Luzhkov and Yeltsin you might do the same thing. We are looking for stability here and there are still, even in Moscow, lots of people who cannot afford market rates for anything."
The government views housing as a key part of its reform programme and says the system of subsidised rents, utilities and other services must be changed to reduce budget handouts.

The government initiative, championed by First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, says rents must rise, but it will target subsidies to the poor so that no one pays more than 25 percent of their income on rent.
But Luzhkov said most people would not be able to afford higher rent, and he pledged to protect Muscovites.

The popular mayor, considered a likely contender for the presidency in 2000, previously won an exemption for Moscow in Russia's privatisation campaign when he accused the government of selling off the country's riches for nothing.
His six-point plan also says Moscow will cut housing costs by inviting firms to tender to provide services like refuse collection and repairs.
Nemtsov's spokesman Andrei Pershin played down the significance of the exemption for Moscow.
"It does not contradict the federal programme which says each region will do what it is able to do," he said.
Low rents -- a one-bedroomed apartment might cost $20 a month if rented from the local authority -- have enabled Russians to survive on average monthly salaries of up to $200.
Larisa Piyasheva, an adviser to the upper house of parliament's budget committee, said it was too early to raise rents.

Piyasheva, Luzhkov's former top aide on privatisation but now a frequent critic, said Russians pay an average of nine percent of their salaries on housing and 52 percent on food, compared to 32 percent and 14 percent in the United States.
"If they change the entire system and raise housing costs, they need to raise salaries so people can continue to eat," she said.
